title: Building a Collaborative Platform Culture in a Bank
gist: At KubeCon & CloudNativeCon Europe, Marcy Paramonova and Stéphane Cusin described how a bank's Kubernetes platform team treated the platform as a collaboration system, using structural rituals (twice-weekly 'Genius Bar', super user awards, user insights sessions) and GitOps self-service to design the culture they wanted. Their core claim: culture follows structure, and embedding principles into the platform makes the desired behavior the easiest path.

insights.claim: A bank's platform team argues an internal platform is not infrastructure but a collaboration system through which much of the organization's communication flows, requiring shared standards between platform and application teams.
insights.speaker: Ben Linders
insights.so_what: Platform engineering value is increasingly framed in organizational terms, supporting demand for tooling that improves cross-team collaboration, not just infra.
insights.locator: A platform is a collaboration system, not infrastructure

insights.claim: Cloud native adoption at the bank was a cultural shift, not only a technical one, and Kubernetes is credited with transforming how the organization builds software, not just its platform.
insights.speaker: Ben Linders
insights.so_what: Regulated enterprises like banks treat Kubernetes adoption as org transformation, implying long, sticky platform investments.
insights.quote: Kubernetes transformed more than our platform. It transformed how our organization builds software
insights.locator: Kubernetes transformed more than our platform

insights.claim: Culture cannot be mandated or left to emerge; teams must design structures and rituals that make desired behaviors natural, and complaints about interruptions indicate a missing structure for people to reach out.
insights.speaker: Ben Linders
insights.so_what: Useful lens for assessing engineering orgs: look for explicit interaction structures rather than stated values.
insights.quote: If your team complains about being interrupted all the time, don’t blame the other team.
insights.locator: Culture follows structure. You cannot wait for culture

insights.claim: The bank's platform team runs a 'Genius Bar' twice a week for two hours per session, where anyone can bring platform questions without a ticket, keeping feedback loops short and surfacing confusing or painful areas quickly.
insights.speaker: Ben Linders
insights.so_what: Replacing ticket-driven support with open sessions is a concrete, low-cost pattern for raising internal platform adoption.
insights.locator: We run a "Genius Bar" twice a week

insights.claim: Open support sessions drew interest beyond developers, including infrastructure, cybersecurity, network, identity and cloud teams, turning support into collaborative problem solving.
insights.speaker: Ben Linders
insights.so_what: Cross-functional pull suggests platform teams can become the coordination hub in large enterprises.
insights.locator: We wanted to step back from the usual support

insights.claim: The platform team introduced super user awards for developers who actively contributed to improving the platform, and credits their sometimes painful feedback with producing a better platform.
insights.speaker: Ben Linders
insights.so_what: Recognition mechanisms for internal contributors are a lever for platform adoption.
insights.locator: Paramonova mentioned that they created events

insights.claim: The team stacks user insights sessions (prioritizing with users rather than for them), demos of shipped and roadmap work, and internal planning sessions, arguing the rhythms together make culture emerge from structure.
insights.speaker: Ben Linders
insights.so_what: Product-management practices applied to internal platforms are becoming standard in platform engineering.
insights.quote: It is not magic, but it is also not accidental.

insights.claim: If every platform action required a ticket, manual intervention or a platform engineer, it would create a culture of dependency in which teams wait instead of learning and operating independently.
insights.speaker: Ben Linders
insights.so_what: Ticket-driven operations are a structural drag on delivery; self-service platforms remove that bottleneck.
insights.locator: If every action required a ticket

insights.claim: The bank's platform capabilities never depend on manual intervention: teams enable capabilities via declarative configuration changes in Git that GitOps applies automatically, giving full traceability of platform adoption.
insights.speaker: Ben Linders
insights.so_what: GitOps-based self-service is being used even in banks, supporting demand for declarative/GitOps tooling in regulated sectors.
insights.locator: One principle we established from day one

insights.claim: Giving every platform feature a lifecycle with visibility into who uses it let the bank safely retire unused features and migrate teams to newer capabilities instead of accumulating complexity.
insights.speaker: Ben Linders
insights.so_what: Usage telemetry on internal capabilities is the enabler for deprecation and reduced platform complexity cost.

insights.claim: Platform capabilities are delivered as versioned artifacts, reusable deployment patterns and documented interfaces rather than one-off team agreements, reinforcing self-service over tickets, standardization over customization, transparency over tribal knowledge and shared ownership over expert dependency.
insights.speaker: Ben Linders
insights.so_what: Embedding principles into the platform makes the desired culture the path of least resistance.
insights.locator: We tried to make platform decisions visible

insights.claim: Using open source with open standards makes engineers' skills highly transferable because they build on a shared foundation across open technologies rather than relearning from zero.
insights.speaker: Ben Linders
insights.so_what: Open-standard stacks lower talent retraining costs, a durable tailwind for open cloud-native ecosystems over proprietary stacks.
insights.locator: When you use open source with open standards

insights.claim: An engineering mindset, defined as the capacity to take on, learn, execute and operate new technologies, matters more than what an engineer knows today.
insights.speaker: Ben Linders
insights.so_what: Hiring and training emphasis shifts toward adaptability as technology churn increases.
insights.locator: An engineering mindset is the most important thing
